# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review: "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

## What the paper claims

**Varden case-processing offices at 24 months:**
- Output per hour is still above control: +9.8% on timesheets and +8.5% on system logs, down from +12.5% at nine months.
- Output per employee is −3.4%, with an interval that includes zero.
- A registered mediation analysis attributes 47% of the per-hour gain to fewer meetings and 18% to lower fatigue.

**Varden counter arm:** stopped at month 12 because of waiting times.

**Halden subset:** 3 of 14 organisations reverted, and the 11 that continued show +11.8% output per actual hour.

**On the earlier documents:** the authors argue that the re-analysis's "entirely an artifact" claim fails, that the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rests on weak studies, and that the meetings mechanism survives a registered test.

## Arithmetic

Nearly everything checks out:
- 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%; 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%.
- Halden: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, so hours fell 13.4%; 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.
- Mediation shares sum to 100%.
- The required counter staffing fits: 1 / 0.886 ≈ +13%, close to the stated 12%.

One figure needs explaining. If 12% more staff restores contacts to control levels, labour cost per contact rises about 12%, not 9%. A 9% figure only works if non-staff costs are in the denominator. State the basis.

## Main issues

**1. The Summary overstates the decline by mixing measures.**
- The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." That compares a timesheet measure at nine months with a log measure at 24 months.
- The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, a fall of about a fifth. Section 3 does this correctly. The Summary should too.
- The decline itself is not tested. The two intervals (+6.9 to +18.4, and +4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily.
- So the data are consistent with some fading, and also with none. "Declined but not disappeared" should become "may have declined somewhat; clearly not disappeared."

**2. What the log measure actually records decides how the mediation should be read.**
- "Active log-in time … working on cases" could mean two different things: time spent working on cases, or total time logged into the system, which would include meetings attended while logged in.
- **If logs capture only case work,** the hours fall should be much smaller than 11%. Meetings fell by about 3.3 hours a week relative to control, so time spent on cases should have fallen only about 3%.
- **If logs capture total presence,** the measure is plausible. But then cutting meetings raises output per log hour partly by simple arithmetic: low-output hours were removed.
- **Baseline:** the authors also need to say whether log data exist for the baseline period. A difference-in-differences estimate needs a pre-period for each measure.

**3. A simple accounting check suggests meetings may explain more than 47% of the gain.**
- **Treated offices.** Baseline is about 37.9 hours, 7.4 of them in meetings, leaving 30.5 hours of other work. A 12% cut in hours is about 4.5 hours, against about 3.3 fewer meeting hours relative to control. Non-meeting time therefore fell only about 1.2 hours, roughly 4%.
- **Output.** Output per FTE fell 3.4%, so output per non-meeting hour is essentially unchanged.
- **Implication.** Read crudely, nearly the whole per-hour gain is accounted for by removing meeting time. Fatigue and unexplained factors would then contribute little.
- **Request.** The mediation model may handle this differently, for example by giving meetings some output value or using a different hours base. The authors should report this accounting decomposition next to the model, and reconcile the two.

**4. The confirmatory test of the meetings hypothesis is not independent.**
- **Same offices.** Registering the test at month 11 rules out flexible analysis choices, which is valuable. But the hypothesis was generated in these same seven treated offices. Re-testing it there is a check that the pattern persisted, not an independent replication. "Survives a registered test" is accurate. Using it to rebut the "post hoc" charge needs that qualification.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information available. Months within an office are not independent, so there are 14 clusters. The mediation intervals (28–66%, 2–34%) look narrow for 14 clusters. Report the inference method used.
- **Confounding.** Mediation needs no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which the limitations note. Here that is especially demanding: a manager who cuts meetings is plausibly also changing other practices that affect output.
- **Baseline meeting data.** The nine-month report had meeting data only for month six. This paper reports baselines of 7.4 versus 7.2. If these were extracted retrospectively from calendars, say so. It is an important addition: it resolves the earlier concern that the month-six gap might have existed before the trial.

**5. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the comparison.**
- Two control offices cut meetings in month 15. That shrinks the treated–control contrast for the last nine months, so the 24-month estimate is biased toward zero.
- The likely cause matters too: it may have been inspired by the trial's published findings.
- Report a sensitivity analysis that excludes these two offices, or handles their post-audit months separately.
- The +4.1% figure for these offices is an uncontrolled before–after comparison of six months against six months, the design the authors rightly criticise elsewhere. It deserves only the heavy caveat the paper already gives it.

**6. Earlier issues remain unaddressed.**
- **Small-cluster inference.** With 7 offices per arm, wild-cluster bootstrap or randomisation-inference intervals are still needed.
- **Backlog and timeliness.** Output per FTE is near control, but queue length, time to decision and deadline compliance are still not reported. After two years these are the obvious places where strain would show.
- **Sick days.** The −27% figure still needs normalising by scheduled days, to rule out a mechanical effect of a four-day week.
- **Appeal overturns.** 3.2% versus 3.0% still has no interval. Appeals of decisions made late in the trial may not have been resolved yet.

**7. The Halden section leaves the attrition finding unanswered.**
- **Attrition.** Varga and Holm showed from the microdata that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons. That contradicts the working paper's account. A Halden author co-signs this report, and the issue isn't acknowledged. It should be corrected or explained.
- **Response bias.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Response is likely related to success, which makes the "survivors twice over" problem worse. Say whether the 9 non-responders differ on their original pilot outcomes.
- **How the reversions are described.** "All with client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches the categories. A marketing agency citing client deadlines is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. It is evidence that reversions also happen outside coverage-bound work.
- **What the authors get right.** They rightly treat the 11 continuers' figures as an upper bound for self-selected organisations. That caveat is well put.

## Bearing on the earlier claims

The paper's adjudication is mostly fair:

- **Against "entirely an artifact."** The rebuttal is sound. Varden at 24 months meets nearly every standard the re-analysis recommended: randomisation, records, actual hours, 18 months or more of follow-up, and no attrition of organisations. It still finds a gain whose interval excludes zero. But this is one public employer with 7 offices per arm. The paper should say the claim is refuted for this setting, not for reduced-hours schemes in general. The re-analysis's novelty argument is also partly vindicated by the possible decline, and the paper could acknowledge that more generously.
- **Against "no decay."** The rebuttal is strong. Confirming that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours settles the point I raised in reviewing the meta-analysis. The figure "about a quarter" is closer to a fifth on the like-for-like measure.
- **On the meetings mechanism.** It is better supported than before, but see points 3 and 4. The paper's most important policy observation is that no arm reorganised work without cutting hours. On the accounting above, much of the per-hour gain might be available at 37.5 hours. That makes a trial with a meetings-only arm the most valuable next study, and the paper should say so explicitly.

## Overall

This is a useful follow-up that resolves two of the questions left open earlier: the gain persists to 24 months, and the case for the meetings pathway is stronger than before. The revisions most worth making are:

1. Fix the mixed-measure decline in the Summary, and test whether the decline is real.
2. Define precisely what the log measure records.
3. Reconcile the mediation shares with the simple accounting decomposition.
4. Run a sensitivity analysis for the contaminated control offices.
5. Report backlog and timeliness outcomes.
6. Correct the Halden attrition account.
